evidence_quotes.quote: We study the governance of public good provision in poor communities in Oaxaca, Mexico.
have water, sewerage, electricity, and that are illiterate.
and faster improvements for sewerage from 2000 to 2010.

country.comment: Study examines municipalities in the state of Oaxaca, Mexico.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title, Summary, and Section 1

effect_estimate.comment: Kernel density propensity-score matching ATT estimates on first differences (Δ) and rates of change (%Δ) in the share of municipal households with service across 564 matched Oaxaca municipalities (418 usos, 146 party) show statistically non-significant effects for water coverage across all intervals, but strongly positive and statistically significant gains for sewerage immediately post-reform (1995–2005) in both levels and rate of change, and a positive significant rate of change in 2000–2010. Note: minus signs on some negative coefficients are omitted in the PDF text layer, so signs are cross-checked against the authors' narrative text on PDF pp. 9–10.
effect_estimate.value: Across 564 matched Oaxaca municipalities (418 usos y costumbres vs. 146 party-governed; kernel density matching ATT with B = 1,000 bootstrapped SEs), legal recognition of traditional participatory governance (usos) had small, statistically non-significant effects on municipal household water coverage across all periods (1990–2000: Δ = 0.012, SE = 0.022, t = 0.538; 1995–2005: Δ = 0.041, SE = 0.049, t = 0.836; 2000–2010: Δ = 0.000, SE = 0.054, t = 0.006; 1990–2010: Δ = 0.027, SE = 0.030, t = 0.893; all %Δ non-significant). For household sewerage coverage, usos produced strongly positive, statistically significant gains in 1995–2005 both in levels (Δ = 0.086, SE = 0.034, t = 2.55, p < 0.01) and rate of change (%Δ = 9.05, SE = 2.18, t = 4.15, p < 0.01), and a faster rate of change in 2000–2010 (%Δ = 3.401, SE = 0.871, t = 3.905, p < 0.01; level Δ = 0.008, SE = 0.022, t = 0.371, non-significant), while 1990–2000 (Δ = 0.037, SE = 0.035; %Δ = 1.27, SE = 1.72) and 1990–2010 (Δ = 0.04, SE = 0.049; %Δ = 0.851, SE = 2.99) were non-significant. Usos municipalities also held more open council sessions (ATT = 2.136, SE = 1.137, t = 1.879; Treated = 412, Control = 228).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 9–11, Section 5; Table 4 and Table 5, PDF p. 10; Note 18, PDF p. 13

mechanism_certainty.comment: Appraised under ROBINS-I, the study faces Serious risk of confounding/selection bias because municipalities self-selected into usos y costumbres in 1995 (often formalizing pre-existing de facto customs) and the propensity score model conditions on post-1995 covariates (2000 census population concentration, city distance, GDP, and 1990–2010 indigenous language share), capping certainty at 2 under CODEBOOK.md §9. Mechanism certainty is rated 2 because the authors directly observe and document the participatory governance and enforcement mechanisms (public assembly project ranking, citizen consultation in Table 1, open council sessions in Table 5, mandatory community labor/cargos, and customary sanctions including water disruption) through ethnographic fieldwork and municipal/citizen surveys, while noting in Section 6 that further research is needed to unpack why usos differentially accelerates sewerage and electricity over water.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 4–6, Section 3; Table 1, PDF p. 6; PDF pp. 7–11, Sections 4–6; Table 5, PDF p. 10

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines legal recognition of indigenous participatory governance (usos y costumbres) via public assemblies, citizen consultation, and open council meetings (participation), municipal executive vs. assembly discretion over formula-based federal social infrastructure transfers FISM/FAIS bypassing partisan state bargaining (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, discretion, political_coordination), and customary community monitoring and sanctioning of non-cooperation in tequio/cargos/servicio including disruption of water supply (ENFORCEMENT, sanction, disconnection).
